entries.title: Where Do America’s Colleges Go From Here?
entries.summary: The Trump administration has a new series of questions for colleges about affordability, curriculum, and “national service”—how will they respond? And: W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington in a dubious battle over education, from the Atlantic archives.
entries.content:
The Trump administration has a new series of questions for colleges about affordability, curriculum, and “national service”—how will they respond? And: W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington in a dubious battle over education, from the Atlantic archives.

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

On August 3, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to states and higher-education leaders with instructions to, as McMahon put it, “describe to the American public your commitments to rigorous teaching, pathbreaking research, and national service—commitments that make our universities a bedrock institution of the American republic.”

A request like that would be simple enough if not for the history between the Trump administration and higher education—a relationship that can fairly be described as antagonistic. Case in point: last year’s “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education,” which critics from across the political spectrum argued effectively asked colleges to compromise academic freedom in exchange for privileged, if vague, access to federal funds. There’s also the suite of federal investigations targeting diversity programs on college campuses.

Questioning colleges is normal. There are outstanding concerns about the experience, the education, and the enterprise of higher education: How much does it cost, and is that more than families can pay? Who gets in, and why? Are faculty members treated with dignity? What is college even for? So, although college leaders argue that a few of the concerns voiced in the document are legitimate, they also see within it the bane of Ilium.

Read: A deal that would end universities’ independence

On this week’s Radio Atlantic, I’m joined by Jack Stripling, the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education, to consider higher education in the Trump era, and the purpose of college itself.

I also go back into the Atlantic archives to look at a debate between W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington over their theories of advancement for Black people, and how it should inform our thinking about colleges today.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Jack Stripling: We keep talking about the politics, but when people are saying I don’t know if college is worth it, they’re usually saying I don’t know if it’s worth the money, not I don’t know if it’s worth risking meeting a liberal person.

Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and around the country millions of students are getting ready to head back to school, if they’re not already in class. So today, we need to think about education in uncertain times.

Now, I was always a big fan of the first day of school. In grade school, I’d pick out my clothes the night before, have them sitting and ready next to my bed. My bag was packed with everything I could possibly need, and some things I definitely didn’t. In college, every new year meant new books, new ideas, and new challenges.

But over the last several years, there has been a battle raging for the soul of higher education in America that’s divorced from those idyllic memories—a battle that has many asking what college is supposed to be and whom it is supposed to serve. Earlier this month, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to colleges asking them to respond to a series of questions. Questions about their institutions, their programs, and how they contribute to the American project. The letter gives college leaders one more thing to consider in an era marked by funding woes, by fears of enrollment stagnation and decline, technological advancements, and political pressures.

How will it all play out? And what will school leaders be thinking about throughout the next year?

Jack Stripling is the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education and my former colleague. And he joins me now to discuss.



Let’s get to questions.

Jack, welcome to the show.

Stripling: Adam Harris, so good to catch up with you.

Harris: Absolutely, man. I want to start with this letter that went out to college leaders recently from Education Secretary Linda McMahon that was effectively the administration’s call to action, right? To prod colleges to address what they see as a sort of outstanding concerns—affordability, viewpoint, diversity, right? That is to say, more acceptable, or more acceptance of conservative views on campus, job preparation, among other things. And it’s sort of been billed as a Compact 2.0, sort of building on the Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education that was criticized in 2025.

In The Chronicle, you all referred to it as either an olive branch or a gloved fist.

So, like, which one is it? How are college presidents viewing this?

Stripling: Well, I think that the backstory is important here, Adam, which you know, which is that this is an administration that has essentially been at loggerheads with higher education since day one. The Trump presidency has largely defined its domestic agenda around attacking higher education for its perceived “wokeness.”

So this was no surprise that they were going to head in this direction to some extent. They have used, as you know, different types of leverage against all sorts of universities: withholding money, threatening all sorts of things. But the one thing they did do last fall was to release this compact for higher education, which was to say Sign on to these federal priorities and we will, in exchange, give you favorable treatment for federal funding. And this was a total flop. No one really signed on to this thing. There were lots of objections to it. And I think where it really hurt this administration was college presidents saying, This isn’t even merit-based, and you’re supposed to be the merit people. You’re now saying you’re going to give favoritism to people who agree with you politically.

So there was a disconnect between two value systems of the Trump administration. So they end up going back to the drawing board and, as you say, this August 3 letter comes from Secretary Linda McMahon that’s called “a national call to action.”

It’s a little softer. It’s more coalition-y, to make a phrase here. It’s based on feedback from influential higher-ed leaders, although some of them seem to be distancing themselves from their role in this.

Harris: Wait, how so?

Stripling: Well, so, one case in point being the Association of American Universities. So this is the group of high-powered research institutions in this country. It’s an invite-only group; it’s very elite to be a part of it. And they have apparently been working behind the scenes in conversations with the Education Department and with the White House about what they would or wouldn’t want to see in such a letter, but they’ve distanced themselves in saying, Hey, we actually didn’t get to take home drafts. We only had these conversations in person, and some of what we said showed up in there, some of it didn’t.

Other people, like the president of Wash U, Andrew Martin, who I think is considered somebody who’s kind of in the “Trump has a point” camp, has said, Hey, I didn’t I didn’t draft this thing, but it does look like some of the things I said are resonating with the Trump administration and ended up in there. But that tells you something about how prickly this is, Adam.

So people want to look like they’re playing ball with the Trump administration, but then they have to answer to other constituencies who are deeply skeptical of the motives behind this quote, unquote “agreement” or “value exercise.”

Harris: One of the things I noticed as you mentioned is that you had not only liberal groups, academics who might skew a little bit more to the left criticizing this original compact, but you also had conservative think tanks who would say things like At least the previous attempts to change higher education had some sort of legal backing, some sort of legal argument. It was a Title VI, it was a Title IX, it was a Title IV. Is this compact different than things that we had seen in previous administrations?

Stripling: Well, I probably should have said more about what was in it, Adam, right? So some of these things are sort of the greatest hits of the Trump administration. They want institutions to answer questions about, like, how are you gonna ensure merit-based admissions? Well, this is a very conservative-coded phrase, right? Because the suspicion is that they’re giving advantages to minority applicants, etc., even though the Supreme Court has said they can’t. So what are you doing on that front? What are you doing to ensure intellectual diversity in your departments? This is another conservative bailiwick, that certain soft sciences and other disciplines are now dominated by left-wing radicals who are here to indoctrinate your children. So they want you to speak to that.

These have flavors of things that came in the old compact. I think the distinction here, though, is that they are saying rather than Sign on to all of this, it’s phrased more in questions. Put something in a public statement that says what you’re doing on this front.

I talked to one former college president recently who said Is the Trump administration going to consider it a win if a bunch of us change our websites? And I think that remains to be seen. Would a symbolic victory of that kind be enough for the Trump administration?

Harris: And is there a concern that if they do put something on the website, the administration might try to poke holes in it?

Stripling: Absolutely, yes.

There are several people that I’ve talked to in recent days who talk about this as a Trojan horse. Because you can’t divorce this from history, Adam.

So I had one former president—I’m not going to name names here—but from a high-profile institution tell me, Well, Jack, you know, what if this came from Obama or Biden? Would people be freaking out about this? And then said, Now set aside all of the things that the Trump administration has done that appear to be or probably are patently unconstitutional and illegal. Set aside the fact that they had their fangs out for higher education from day one.

Well, you really can’t, right? You can’t set that aside. There’s history here, and so there’s a complete lack of trust. And the idea that we’re gonna put a public statement on our website saying we ostensibly sign on to a lot of the things you like—there’s great suspicion about how that information might be used against the institutions at some later date.

Harris: But we’ve seen some institutions comply, right, and already respond to the administration. So who has been responding and what are they saying in their responses to the call to action?

Stripling: The early responses are coming from pretty expected quarters. So Florida’s universities and state colleges, as well as the University of North Carolina system. These are both university systems that have a lot of political and ideological alignment with the Trump administration. They’re governed by boards that are led by Republicans or people with deep ties to the party. So it’s not really surprising to see them come out. They both praise the secretary’s questions. You know, we were waiting to be asked. Thank you so much. And they said We’re already doing a lot of the work that the Trump administration cares about.

So things like cracking down on disruptive protesters or banning DEI-related measures or emphasizing civics education. This is all pretty standard policy, particularly in red states now at public universities, so that’s not a big surprise. They were also asked about things that I think are arguably pretty nonpartisan, like dealing with grade inflation, maintaining academic rigor in the AI age. These are things that universities across the country, regardless of politics, I think, are concerned about and thinking about, so they weighed in on that.

I think what’s distinct in the responses to this letter from these two states, at least, though, is the highly nationalistic tone. They’re being pressed to talk about how they will serve American interest. And these states are very comfortable with that type of conversation, perhaps in a way that left-leaning faculty, frankly, might not be. Florida’s saying, Hey, we’re capping undergrads from foreign countries. That’s one of the things we’re doing. UNC says We emphasize research related to national defense. It’s probably a bit rah-rah for some in the faculty set. It reminds me a little bit of post-9/11 America, what we saw in higher education after that. But I think to sort of sum it up, Florida and North Carolina are saying You’re preaching to the choir here. In fact, you’re preaching to the choir directors. We were already on this. And so it’s not surprising to hear this from them.

Harris: But it’s almost like serving up a little bit of red meat with a little bit of substance.

Stripling: I think so, I think so. This has been compared to what people do in an accreditation process, for example. We know the rules; this is how we’re obeying them. And it’s, you know, it’s sort of a statement of alignment as much as anything.

Harris: Yeah. And so for these states, which are functionally sort of aligned ideologically, they’re saying that they are already concerned about these things. They’re already working on these things. And you mentioned that other institutions are concerned about these things. Are they also working on those things? Like, how much of this is the rest of higher education already doing?

Stripling: Well, I think that we’re having a national conversation around things like the SAT, for example. Some colleges went test optional, or even test blind. And even, you know, the liberal state of California is starting to grapple with this question. Did doing away with the SAT mean that we got students here who weren’t prepared for the level of work they were going to get at a University of California campus? So that conversation is happening in states red and blue, and it’s something the Trump administration emphasizes and cares deeply about.

It’s part of this larger merit conversation.

Harris: And of the things that are in the actual call to action, how much of it are colleges already doing? I thought that was a really interesting critique, was that these questions are things that we’ve already outlined; they’re things we’re already trying to address. So how much of it are the colleges actually already doing?

Stripling: Well, your mileage may vary on whether they’re doing enough to control cost, whether they’re doing enough to address ideological capture within their own departments.

Cost you can’t argue with; we now have from the highly selective institutions that are charging over $100,000 to other privates that are much lower but still very much out of reach for most American families. Very hard to argue with that.

Then you have recent reports from Yale and one commissioned by the chancellors at Vanderbilt and Wash U that have both said there’s some credence to this idea that politicization has become a problem in our academic departments. So those voices are coming from within. Clearly there has been some recognition within higher education that some of these critiques have some merit.

Harris: To that point though, one of the administration’s plans, goals, is to address the high cost of going to college. But how much control do institutions actually have over the cost of education?

Jack Stripling: Well, Adam, you’ll know from our days working together at The Chronicle, which were the best of my life, I should say—2017 was a great year for me.

Harris: Incredible. I enjoyed it so much.

Stripling: But in any case, you’ll remember it was the same story that we were hearing then, which was that a lot of the drivers of cost have to do with personnel; they have to do with structural issues within higher education; they have to do with students wanting more amenities—that was kind of an old sall. And I think you’re hearing a lot of the same things, but the fact is they can’t get away from the reality that people are losing confidence in higher education as an institution.

If you look at the latest polling on this, I think it’s, like, four in 10 Americans that say they have high confidence or a lot of confidence in higher education now. And even Democrats who have historically supported higher education more than Republicans are starting to lose their affection for the institution.

So I think there’s a recognition that it’s a real problem, and I really do think that the money is the big factor. We keep talking about the politics, but when people are saying I don’t know if college is worth it, they’re usually saying I don’t know if it’s worth the money, not I don’t know if it’s worth risking meeting a liberal person.

Harris: I do want to talk more about the purpose of higher education, but I wanted to ask first about the pressures for ideological change from the administration and state lawmakers. You’re in Florida, and that’s a good example of the changes in terms of curriculum, institutional culture. So are you noticing any effects?

Stripling: I think it kind of remains to be seen, Adam. I still—and again, this is really more gut than data—but I still do think cost is the major thing families are worried about.

I will say that, to your point, I do live in Florida and, you know, this is famously the place where woke goes to die, as Ron DeSantis said. And a lot of action has been taken on the ideological front that is also connected to this question of What is college for?

So if you think about the core curriculum, the courses that colleges are saying everybody should take, there’s usually some menu of sorts. A lot of institutions over time—there’s been a lot of bloat there. There’s been a lot of things that we might not consider essential that have come into the core curriculum. So some of these ostensibly sort of ideological attacks resonate to some degree with faculty who say, Actually we have gotten a little out of control in what’s in this core.

But what you’re pointing to, Adam, is the key distinction, which is, is higher education about vocation or does it have some sort of more aspirational mission? And this is an old problem. Are you there to learn about how to prepare for your first job, or is it about preparing you for a life of greater intellectual enrichment? And I think that that’s at the heart of a lot of the conversations we’re having, even if they are politically coded. What is college for? continues to be something that, you know, sort of divides people.

What’s interesting is that parents and even students will tell you, I really want to go to college and be able to get a good job. And I want to be able to leave here with a credential that matters and that is seen as authentic, even though I use ChatGPT for half my classes.

But students also say they want more. If you look at the studies around mental health that places like the Harvard Grad School of Education have done, they are desperate for something real. And so when they come to an institution that seems like it’s all about pleasing the next corporate overlord, they chafe. That’s why they’re booing at commencement ceremonies when people praise AI, right? So students actually do want something more than something to punch up their résumé.

Harris: So, Jack, we’re in August, whole school year ahead of us. What will you be keeping your eye on the most as this year develops?

Stripling: I go back to what I said before, which is this collective sense of Is the Trump administration done with us?

I think that that is something that I’m starting to hear people in higher education ask. Like, Was this Act 1, or is this letter in and of itself a form of surrender, a sort of concession? They’re looking for a symbolic win. Using the DOJ and these other arms of the government to try to exact concessions or revenge is very expensive. It’s very time consuming, and they’ve lost in court in some big ways. Now these cases are still unfolding, but that’s the reality.

What I will be paying attention to is this question of purpose, though. And I know this is going to sound weird, Adam, but have you read Stoner?

Harris: Yes, I have.

Stripling: Okay. So for folks who don’t know, this is a 1965 novel by John Williams. We just talked about it on my podcast, College Matters. We had sort of a reading club.

And it’s the story about this professor at Mizzou, who’s this farm boy who goes to the University of Missouri thinking that he’s going to major in some kind of agricultural sciences. He’s going to come back and work on the family farm, and life’s gonna be happy for him and his parents. What ends up happening instead is that he goes into this class and he’s exposed to his first Shakespearean sonnet, and it immediately changes his world. He can’t explain why, but the way he sees people, the way he sees worlds, the way he interacts with the universe changes in some profound way. And the frustration of the novel is that he can’t really explain it to anyone. It’s just something he feels.

And that’s the problem with this product that we call “higher education.” When it works as it should, it’s transformational. It changes you in profound ways. But it’s nearly impossible to explain how.

And that makes it really hard to charge $100,000 for. And so what higher education is going to have to do this year, like it has every other previous year I’ve been covering it, is explain that transformational experience in a way that resonates with every constituency, whether it’s the Trump administration, the student who doesn’t have enough money to go to college, the parents who are skeptical about the the job return, the people who care about AI and how that’s changing credentials. Somehow they’re going to have to make that case, and maybe reading Stoner is a good start. But that’s what I’m always thinking about.

Harris: Well, Jack, as always, it is fantastic to see you, to talk to you, and you’ve given us a lot to think about as we head into this new school year. It’s great to have you on.

Stripling: Thank you, Adam. Let’s do it again. I really appreciate it.

Harris: We’re back in the archives this week with a look at a question that has troubled some of the greatest minds throughout history. It’s a question that Booker T. Washington and W. E. B. Du Bois tried to answer in The Atlantic between 1896 and 1903: Are colleges designed only to train people to work for their own improvement, or are they designed to train people to create a better society?

Booker T. Washington was the most powerful Black man of the late 19th and early 20th century in America. He was born on a tobacco plantation in 1856, and he was emancipated from slavery at the end of the Civil War. He was 9 years old then. Education changed his life.

Writing about his upbringing in the September 1896 issue of The Atlantic, Washington said: “After the close of the war, while working in the coal-mines of West Virginia for the support of my mother, I heard in some accidental way of the Hampton Institute.”

Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute, near the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia, had opened its doors in 1868. It had a simple mission: “to train selected Negro youth who should go out and teach and lead their people first by example.” The students from Hampton were expected to get land and homes, to work for their money with knowledge of why they were doing the work—or, as the institution’s founder put it, “to replace stupid drudgery with skilled hands.”

Washington would later write in the pages of The Atlantic in 1896 the education he received at Hampton changed him, it “caused me for the first time to realize what it meant to be a man instead of a piece of property.”

He was ready to proselytize, to spread the word on this industrial, practical education that wasn’t just a mirror of what was popular. It wasn’t just teaching French for the sake of saying that it did or the piano while expecting nothing but a future of poverty in return for its graduates. It was a functional education, which would help Black people less than a generation removed from slavery learn the skills they needed to advance.

In 1881, Washington went to the Deep South, to the Black Belt in Alabama, to establish a school in Tuskegee. The school opened with one teacher, 30 students, and not a lick of property to speak of save a shanty and a church. But Washington was a savvy dealer; he coaxed donations from wealthy people in both the North and the South by preaching a philosophy of self-reliance. The students worked to build buildings on campus while they received an industrial education. And by the time he was writing in The Atlantic in 1896, that little college in Tuskegee had grown to 800 students, taught by 79 faculty members, spread across 1,400 acres of land which housed 30 buildings.

Washington’s reputation grew alongside the institution, not least because of what he was willing to set aside to achieve his goal.

His philosophy would have allowed—at least in the short term—the continuation of Black Americans’ second-class citizenship.

Black people, Washington argued in his Atlantic essay, were to find their dignity through their industrial labors and the financial gains it brought them. He wrote that “it is through the dairy farm, the truck garden, the trades, and commercial life, largely, that the negro is to find his way to the enjoyment of all his rights.”

Now, despite the critique that Washington’s school only taught Black people to do the same jobs that they did during slavery, even his critics were forced to admire his brilliance and thrift and ability to make a tangible difference in the lives of Black people in the Black Belt.

Perhaps most prominent among those critics was W. E. B. Du Bois, who argued that the training students received at Tuskegee was necessary but insufficient on its own. Sure, it might lead to the economic advancement for some of its students; it might make them self-sufficient, able to eat and clothe themselves. But Du Bois argued that there was more to life than food and clothing.

Du Bois thought a true college education—a liberal education of the kind taught at Fisk, Atlanta University, Wilberforce, Howard, and Lincoln, among others—was the foundation of advancement. In the September 1902 issue of The Atlantic, Du Bois argued that there needed to be teachers for would-be students. Those colleges like Fisk that were training Black people to go back and teach their kin were of the highest importance. Du Bois wrote: “In a single generation they put thirty thousand black teachers in the South; they wiped out the illiteracy of the majority of the black people of the land, and they made Tuskegee possible.”

The schools Du Bois praised developed not only workers but full men. They produced people capable of critical thought. The Bible says that man shall not live by bread alone; Du Bois had his own version. “We shall hardly induce black men to believe that if their bellies be full it matters little about their brains.”

The reality that both men acknowledged is that both forms of teaching—the one that begins with the theoretical and the other with the practical—are necessary to improve the situation for Black people in America, to unwind the damage done by generations of laws which banned Black education.

Washington thought enough of his critics to respond, which he did in the October 1903 issue of The Atlantic, where he wrote: “I cannot understand how any reasonable person can object to such education for a large part of a people who are in the poverty-stricken condition that is true of a large element of my race, especially when such hand training is combined, as it should be, with the best education of the head and heart.”

But the issue was that Washington’s idea of a practical education which would disregard social equality was weaponized: It was treated as the only way rather than a way.

As Du Bois noted in his 1902 essay, “I sit with Shakespeare and he winces not. Across the color line I move arm in arm with Balzac and Dumas, where smiling men and welcoming women glide in gilded halls.” Reading the classics gave him a sense of the ties that bind humanity; they welcomed him to the great brotherhood of mankind.

The question animating the debate between Washington and Du Bois is as relevant as ever: Is college meant to train people for the workforce of today or to produce graduates capable of building a better tomorrow? It’s a question that we should all be considering.

That’s all for today’s show.

This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli.

It was edited by Hadley Robinson.

It was engineered by Miguel Carrascal and has original music by Rob Smierciak.

Claudine Eibed is the executive producer of Atlantic Audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday.

You can subscribe on The Atlantic’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts.

And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues you can subscribe to the publication at theatlantic.com/listener.

Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

entries.title: The Atlantic announces Jessica Goldstein as SVP of events
entries.summary: Goldstein joins after leading events at NPR and the Skoll Foundation
entries.content:
Goldstein joins after leading events at NPR and the Skoll Foundation

The Atlantic has hired Jessica Goldstein as senior vice president of events, who will work in partnership with managing director for events Evan Smith to lead and produce the magazine’s robust live programs nationwide. She begins with The Atlantic in early September.

Jessica has spent her career telling stories through reporting and creating live experiences that resonate far beyond the stage. She spent eight years creating and leading NPR’s live cultural programming, including creating the Tiny Desk Contest, NPR’s annual search for new musical talent, and the How I Built This Summit. She most recently led the Skoll Foundation’s global convenings strategy and directed the Skoll World Forum.

At The Atlantic, she will work with Evan to lead one of the most influential and long-running events practices in media. The Atlantic convenes dozens of annual in-person and virtual events that reach thousands of people every year, anchored by its flagship event, The Atlantic Festival, which returns to New York City September 17–19, after being held for nearly two decades in Washington, D.C. The Atlantic is also under way with a new 50-state tour, The Atlantic Across America, that has already held events in 10 states, addressing some of the most complex issues of our time.

Below is Evan Smith’s announcement to staff:

I’m excited to let you know that we’ve hired the amazing Jessica Goldstein as our new senior vice president of events. As the second-in-command on our growing team, she’ll oversee the operations, planning, and execution of our robust public programs, working closely with our sales, marketing, design, and CSG colleagues to grow The Atlantic’s audience and revenue; shine a great, big light on our brand; and—most crucially—bring our journalists and our journalism to stages from coast to coast through The Atlantic Festival, The Atlantic Across America, The Atlantic Summits, and so much more.

Jessica comes to us most recently from the Skoll Foundation, where she was managing director of convenings, leading the organization’s global events strategy and directing the Skoll World Forum, a weeklong gathering of heads of state, social entrepreneurs, and civil-society partners. But it’s her reputation at NPR that really precedes her—and makes her the ideal hire in this moment. As senior director and executive producer of Events & Experiential, she spent eight years creating and leading NPR’s live programming, including the Tiny Desk Contest and the How I Built This Summit. Previously she was a senior supervising producer for NPR Music, a senior producer on the science desk, and a producer of audio documentaries known as NPR Radio Expeditions. A native of New York, Jessica is a graduate of the University of Wisconsin at Madison.

Jessica believes in the power of storytelling, of sharing ideas and sparking inspiration, which is precisely how we think about our work in the events space. There is no loftier task before us than getting people from divergent backgrounds—great minds who don’t think alike—in a room to listen and talk and continue the conversation after we’re gone. She will bring to bear her decades of experience, her imagination, her creativity, her calm, and her charisma as we expand the ambitious work of the Live team.

entries.title: A Reverse Ellis Island
entries.summary: A city at the southern tip of Mexico has become the place where migrants’ dreams go to die.
entries.content:
A city at the southern tip of Mexico has become the place where migrants’ dreams go to die.

Julio Borrell knew he was being deported, but after 47 hours on a bus rattling through Mexico, he still had no idea where the United States was sending him. Through the window, he saw the cities give way to sprawling banana plantations and coffee farms. The passengers were still wearing whatever clothes they’d had on when they were detained by ICE: shirts splattered with paint from their most recent job, pajama pants, landscaping-company uniforms, bathing suits. Borrell had lived in Miami for 46 years. Now he watched as the bus passed a sign for the Guatemala border and then pulled over on the side of the road.

“Where are we?” Borrell asked.

“Tapachula,” a Mexican immigration agent answered.

Borrell hadn’t heard of it. Neither had anyone else on the bus. The deportees weren’t from here. They weren’t even from Mexico. They were Cuban, Venezuelan, Nicaraguan, and Haitian—many of them elderly, some stripped of their green card after spending most of their life in the United States. The Trump administration, unable or unwilling to send them to their home country, had bused them 2,000 miles, from the U.S. border to a small city where they don’t have legal status. It’s a practice that started last year without any announcement and has quietly grown since then. “Why the hell did they bring us here?” Borrell, who migrated to Miami from Havana in 1980, asked me while I was in Tapachula this month.

By the time we met, Borrell, a tall, sinewy 72-year-old with a shock of gray hair, had been in Tapachula for about six months, trying to make enough money fixing tires to rent a studio apartment. He knew that a handful of other Cuban deportees had been flown even farther away, to African nations such as Eswatini and South Sudan. But it was Tapachula that had become a mass waiting area for those rebuffed by U.S. immigration policy, out of sight of lawyers and human-rights defenders. This is now where the largest concentration of deportees is dropped in Mexico, and where most migrants traveling through Latin America en route to the U.S. are halted. Donald Trump can claim that the border is “closed” because it has effectively been relocated to Tapachula. The city looks and feels the way towns in northern Mexico along the U.S. border once did—a dumping ground for those expelled from the United States and a gathering place for those snagged on their way north.

Mexican agents pull migrants out of commercial buses and cars on the freeway leaving the city, making sure the deportees don’t attempt to return to the United States. Another set of agents waits for the next busload of Cubans, Venezuelans, and Haitians to arrive so they can be processed. It’s what experts call externalization: the outsourcing of migration management to other countries.

Borrell told me that he’d come to the United States when he was 26 as part of the Mariel boatlift, the mass exodus of Cubans who traveled on crowded boats to Miami in 1980. He had seven American children, 11 grandchildren, and a great-grandchild. He had run a mechanic shop and renewed his visa each time it neared expiration. He could feel his body breaking down after years of physical labor and had been looking forward to retirement and more time with his family in South Florida.

Then, last December, he went to his scheduled immigration check-in, as he had done dozens of times before. This time, he was detained by ICE agents. They sent Borrell to Florida’s Alligator Alcatraz for four months and then to Eloy Detention Center, in Arizona. From there, he was put on a bus for the U.S.-Mexico border and then another, bound for Tapachula. He walked on the side of the road for an hour before borrowing a cellphone to call his family back in Miami. “I’m in some place called Tapachula, Chiapas,” he told his daughter.

Borrell, like thousands of other non-Mexicans deported here, arrived without clear legal status and with nowhere to stay. Many deportees sleep on the street for their first few nights. Mexico denies that it is facilitating deportations from the United States to Tapachula, even though more than a dozen migrants described to me the cooperation between U.S. and Mexican immigration agents in their expulsions. According to data from the Mexican Institute for Migration, 12,977 non-Mexicans were deported to Mexico from January 2025 to March 2026, largely to southern Mexico. They joined the tens of thousands of other migrants from all over the world who have been stranded in Tapachula during their journey to the United States, after being blocked by Mexican immigration agents from moving farther north. The mix of nationalities here has prompted officials at the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration to begin informally referring to the city as TapaYork—a kind of reverse Ellis Island. There are roughly 350,000 permanent residents of Tapachula and approximately 60,000 migrants living here. Some have tried to flee Tapachula multiple times, only to be deported back over and over again after being caught by Mexican agents.

U.S. officials have consistently said that their goal is “zero border crossings”—a more absolutist project than Trump articulated during his first term, when it was easier for migrants to advance beyond Tapachula. This month, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed that his department was accomplishing that goal. (Crossings are indeed way down, but they’re not at zero.) In meetings with their Mexican counterparts, U.S. officials continue to ask for more stringent immigration enforcement and accommodation for long-distance deportations, according to Mexican officials. The Mexicans, who fear unilateral U.S. military action, have generally complied. The Cubans, Venezuelans, and Haitians who are expelled here in buses that typically arrive a few times a week are evidence of Mexico’s acquiescence. In addition to the buses filled with foreigners, Tapachula’s tiny airport sometimes receives as many as five flights of Mexican deportees a day. (There have been more than 196 so far this year.) Most of the Mexicans arriving by plane head straight to the local bus station and return to their home state or to the border again. Some are minors and need to wait for their parents to pick them up.

In his first weeks here, Borrell, disoriented, was walking to an ATM to see whether he could withdraw cash when he saw a face he recognized. It was a Cuban friend from Miami, who ran a tile business.

“What are you doing here, man?” Borrell asked.

His friend, who had moved to the U.S. from Cuba when he was 6 and held a green card, had also been deported by bus. Borrell told him what he has said many times since: “We’ve got to get out of here. I’m not going to die in Tapachula.”

From his small stand selling bread in downtown Tapachula, Mervil Wisdael, 43, sees the groups of deportees arrive a few times a week. “They’re lost,” he told me. “They’re just dragging their feet. They don’t even know where they are.”

Wisdael, from Port-au-Prince, is part of a different population of migrants here, one that intended to pass through on the way to the United States. Tapachula has historically been a way station for migrants traveling north, including those who navigated the jungle of Panama’s Darién Gap before continuing to Mexico. I spent a week in Tapachula in 2018, when a caravan of migrants amassed there on their way north, early in Trump’s first term. Migrants slept in the central plaza, in the bus station, in rented rooms and shelters. It quickly became a media spectacle. Trump claimed that the group leaving Tapachula, which included many young Central American families, was full of criminals. He demanded that Mexico intercept them. A few days later, I walked with the migrants to the edge of the town, where Mexican immigration authorities had blocked the road. Hundreds of people were detained. Taking a break, one officer said to me, “We’re doing what your president asked.”

Since then, the Mexican government has again and again bent to the will of the U.S. government on immigration enforcement. It signed off on the “Remain in Mexico” policy in 2019, which forced asylum seekers to wait for their immigration appointments from Mexico’s northern border rather than from within the United States. Under the Joe Biden–era CBP One program, it agreed to host asylum seekers even farther south, including in Tapachula. Then, during Trump’s second term, Mexico agreed to mass deportations to the city. Mexican officials told me that the main consideration for the Americans was Tapachula’s distance from the U.S. border and the way agents could create a choke hold on the only highway leaving the city. I came back to Tapachula to see how that series of capitulations had changed the city, a gritty commercial hub surrounded by miles of farmland, where near-daily afternoon storms briefly break the tropical heat.

Read: A planeload of informants

Wisdael had planned to make his way to the U.S. to reunite with his family and apply for asylum. But by the time he arrived in Tapachula, six years ago, Mexico was no longer allowing migrants to transit through the country without a humanitarian visa or refugee status, which could take months or years to get. He stayed until he got his papers, and then he waited longer to see whether it might get easier to cross the U.S. border. Many other Haitians stayed too. Roughly 10 percent of the city’s public-school students are now from Haiti. Each of its three semiprofessional basketball teams has Haitian players. The city’s market is peppered with stalls selling Haitian food. Employees of the municipal immigration office have taught themselves Creole.

Wisdael has been in Tapachula longer than most of his countrymen. He speaks fluent Spanish. He met a Guatemalan woman, Ericka Leonardo, while working on a construction crew there. She was walking down the street.

“You’re pretty,” he said.

“I’ve never dated a Black guy,” she said.

“Maybe you should try,” he said.

They’re now married and live together in Tapachula. She works at an arcade around the corner from his bread stall. They’ve become informal sources of information about Mexico’s archaic immigration system. Wisdael explains to newly arrived Haitians that they need to line up at Mexico’s refugee office every 15 days so that a bureaucrat can sign a document proving that they have not absconded from Tapachula. After 30 or 40 or 50 signatures—anywhere from one to two years—most Haitians will have refugee status in Mexico. “They don’t want to wait that long. No one wants to wait that long here,” he said.

But Wisdael knows that it’s not a good time to attempt to cross the U.S. border. Most people don’t even get that far. Haitians without Mexican papers are typically caught by Mexican immigration agents at a checkpoint just north of Tapachula. The city once felt like a stepping stone. Now it feels like a dead end.

Almost every immigrant community in Tapachula has its own Wisdael—someone who has been around long enough to explain the rules to the newly arrived. Aside from the Cubans and Venezuelans, there are thousands of Central Americans, along with smaller groups of Congolese, Senegalese, Bangladeshis, and Nepalese. There’s a Cameroonian bar and a Ghanaian restaurant within walking distance of the 19th-century colonial church in the city center. The man guarding the door at one of the migrant shelters is Ukrainian. Most people have learned just enough Spanish to ask at least two questions: How long have you been here? And when are you leaving?

Before I left Tapachula, I was curious to meet the city employees running the municipal migrant-assistance center. I followed directions to a mostly abandoned covered market at the edge of town. I was sure I was lost. Then an enthusiastic 28-year-old, Kevin Figueroa, leapt out of his office holding a laptop. He had a PowerPoint presentation on migration in Tapachula. Did I want to see it?

He flipped through the slides on the large numbers of migrant arrivals here and all of the ways the city had integrated them into municipal life. I knew that there had been protests over the past few years by locals upset about the way their city was changing. In 2022, Roberto Fuentes, the city council’s general secretary, told reporters that “the city is in a state of siege, a state of chaos.” At least once, Haitian street vendors like Wisdael have been physically removed from the city center by local police.

But Figueroa assured me that Tapachulans had become accustomed to the way their city had been transformed. The economy was growing. The food was better. I partially believed him. In some ways, the city did seem to have settled into its new demographics. But there were still frequent confrontations between migrants and municipal employees—triggered, for example, by migrants using public electricity outlets to charge their phones. This month, several migrants set their mattresses on fire in the city’s migrant-detention center, leading the military to intervene. Two Venezuelans were arrested. Mexico’s immigration agency said obliquely in a press release that the protest was in response to “the dissatisfaction of a group of foreign nationals regarding their immigration process.”

What seems to bother those trapped in Tapachula most is not the way they are treated in the city, but that they are here at all, in a no-man’s-land, far from any place they ever lived. It’s an approach the Trump administration plans to expand to more remote locations. Not long after I left Tapachula, the Liberian government announced that it would accept 1,200 non-Liberian deportees from the United States. Such an announcement would, until recently, have been a radical departure from decades of immigration policy. But there has been little outcry. The U.S. has kept the desperation of deportees and asylum seekers at a great distance. Some of the Cubans I spoke with in Tapachula told me that in the next week or two, they will begin marching north in their own migrant caravan. They know their chances of getting to the border are close to zero. But they think the effort might be enough to remind Americans that they are there, waiting at the southern tip of Mexico.

entries.title: A Freedom 250 Event That Actually Worked
entries.summary: Other patriotic spectacles this summer felt like Trump rallies. This was a car race.
entries.content:
Other patriotic spectacles this summer felt like Trump rallies. This was a car race.

An interest in the thrills of car racing is not what drove me to spend my Sunday afternoon at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, the latest of the spectacles that Donald Trump has presided over during the United States’ big birthday celebrations all summer. I was there yesterday because I was worried about art. The event involved 25 cars zipping around a number of D.C.’s museums and historic buildings at worryingly high speeds—147 times. Preservationists and conservators had raised concerns ahead of the contest, leading me to imagine creaking sculptures and rattling ceramics, all because the president wanted a race around the National Mall. Seeing the National Gallery of Art’s huge black Alexander Calder sculpture outside, surrounded by wood boards as if the poor thing were hunkering down for war, didn’t help.

But it turns out that playing art patrol is rather difficult at an IndyCar race, especially when you find yourself crammed into a sweaty crowd as blurs of color whiz by. This proximity to the action means you are a participant in a much more visceral way than at many other sporting events: You can feel the vibrations in your toes. Somewhere among the vrooms, I realized that this was not like the other Freedom 250 productions I had attended, like the Great American State Fair with its drab triumphal arch and the Freedom Trucks with their selective history. Instead, in some moments, the Grand Prix was … fun?

The good vibes began when I spotted the driver Sting Ray Robb’s maintenance truck, decorated with the ridiculously wholesome image of seven puppies climbing on his race car. He immediately gained a fan in me, though he crashed early on. The course, with its many bumps, was tricky for drivers, and just more than half of them even finished. Kyle Kirkwood, another American, won.

Many might be tempted to slot the IndyCar race next to other Trumpian events that have disrupted life in the nation’s capital. More than that, the race could easily serve as another example of how little an administration that has pressured museums and diluted historic-preservation laws cares for the nation’s cultural heritage. These interpretations aren’t overblown.

Earlier this year, the Grand Prix unveiled (and later walked back) a disturbing T-shirt that featured a white-clad figure and read: One Nation One Race. In and around the city yesterday, the traffic was a pain for locals, the nearest airport had to stop flights for three hours, and the noise—including multiple deafening flyovers—was nothing short of a public nuisance. For those without tickets, access to the Mall was closed off. Madhan Subramanian, who lives by the course, told me he was “just a little annoyed by everything.” He thought it was a cool event, but “it was harder to get groceries and just do our normal thing.”

The worries about vibrations and damage to artifacts were legitimate, too. In the middle of the race, I put my hand on the boarded-up geometric I. M. Pei skylights outside the National Gallery and found them shaking like a cellphone on vibrate. (Not great!) A man yelled to me over the thunderous cars, “Are we okay?” I replied, in earnest, “I’m not sure.” (So far, there have been no reports of damaged art.)

Reckless is one word for what unfolded in the capital yesterday. But one person’s reckless is another’s exciting. And the Freedom 250 Grand Prix certainly had oomph to it. Trump did a lap of the track at the beginning of the race to the sound of mixed cheers and boos, and although I noticed Trump gear—Trump 2028 hats, for example—for sale outside the race perimeter, inside many fans had opted for checkers and race jerseys.

In other words, this didn’t feel like another Freedom 250 event that was more about Trump than about America. Race-car driving occupies its own indomitable universe of fandom, kitsch, design, and hype. Ultimately, a race is a race, and many in the crowd appeared to be there simply for the sport.

Keith Cole, a former amateur racer and F1 fan, was among them. A car race in downtown Washington seemed like a once-in-a-lifetime thing, so he came to D.C. with a friend despite some low-grade partisan energy they didn’t care for. “We don’t see a lot of people like us here,” Cole, who is Black, told me, noting some MAGA-hat sightings, too. “I understand how they want to use it to politicize it, but this is sports. You gotta, kind of, take it out of it.”

Most of the time, the National Mall is a reflective space flanked by quiet, regal buildings that command a certain respect. Yesterday, though, America’s “front yard” felt more like a backyard. IndyCar fans played cornhole and giant Connect Four on the grass, which was dotted with lemonade stands and picnic tables. In one moment, I was surrounded by beer-drinking racing fanatics; in the next, I was engulfed in the smell of gasoline and the sound of revving engines; minutes later, after a short stroll, I was standing in the National Gallery in front of a Georgia O’Keeffe.

Inside one of the galleries, I found Carol Madden—a native of Indianapolis, IndyCar’s namesake and the site of its premier event, the 500—seeking a break from the heat near some Renaissance-era earthenware. “The Indy 500 is Christmas for my family. We don’t come home for Christmas and Easter—we all come home for the race,” she told me. This was her 55th race, which she attended with her whole family, she said, getting teary-eyed.

Nearby, Diana Vinson, as much a race-car fan as a museum lover, was immersed in a photograph on the wall. She didn’t see her appreciation for the two things as entirely separate. Both art and racing are all about precision; they’re about tiny decisions—in brushstrokes or tire pressure—that add up. “You have to understand your mediums,” she told me.

The museum was making the most of any connection it could find with the event, which forced it to partially close for the race; the portion of it that remained open was accessible only to IndyCar ticket holders. (The National Gallery has been notably savvy about garnering attention of late, as evidenced by its viral videos of a Gen Z–whispering senior curator who called that Renaissance earthenware “bussin’.”) Outside, signs promised “iconic art (and air-conditioning).” Staff members had set up a tent where they sold T-shirts featuring a portrait of George Souders, who won the Indy 500 in 1927, from the museum’s collection.

Earlier, out on the Mall, I had spoken with Bill Sherman, a fan of “anything that makes noise and goes fast,” who told me he thinks people are drawn to car racing because they can see themselves in it. “I’ve driven these roads hundreds of times,” he said. “It’s one of the few sports that you can look at and say, I can go out and do that every day on the Beltway.”

Though that would certainly spice up your commute, you shouldn’t. Just like you shouldn’t send thousands of pounds of metal flying around historic sites. But watching cars hurtling past the National Archives, barreling toward the Air and Space Museum, with the U.S. Capitol looming in the distance, you might just convince yourself otherwise.

entries.title: What a Bicentennial Baby Knows
entries.summary: When I was born, the moniker carried a sheen of optimism. So much feels different now.
entries.content:
When I was born, the moniker carried a sheen of optimism. So much feels different now.

This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.

Thirteen seconds after midnight on July 4, 1976, Karen Steele was born in Montclair, New Jersey, and was anointed the first “bicentennial baby.” Newspaper articles followed. President Gerald Ford and his wife, Betty, sent a note to the family. And then it kind of became a thing. Any baby born that year was treated like they had emerged playing the fife and drums. In Mobile, Alabama, new mothers received a commemorative blanket. In Covington, Louisiana, a hospital handed out (for $2.50) special “bicentennial baby” certificates on faux parchment, a “memento that can be framed and cherished as a family heirloom for endless generations.”

This was a year of jaw-dropping kitsch, an explosion of red, white, and blue everything—toilet paper, lollipops, even condoms (pleading: One Time for Old Glory). Branding newborns this way became part of the general patriotic fun. And although the tchotchkes surely ended up moldering in a red, white, and blue landfill somewhere, the label stuck. I know: I was one of those babies, born in August 1976.

Being a bicentennial baby was not anything I ever thought about all that much. In fact, it was really only when meeting another person born in 1976 that it came up at all. Oh, you’re a bicentennial baby too, one of us would say to the other, smiling dumbly. This was a secret handshake that opened zero doors. But unlike other indelible parts of my identity that felt small in their particularity—like being the child of immigrants or being nearsighted—having my birth hitched somehow to the history of the country, to its forward motion, felt big whenever I was reminded of it.

Beyond the horror of realizing that five of my current lifespans stacked up is all that separates me now from Benjamin Franklin, I’ve been thinking about this cohort of which I’m a part. Expounding on the significance of one’s own generation can lead rapidly to wild generalization, self-absorption, and some misplaced nostalgia. I know this. But I’m convinced that my fellow bicentennial babies and I have been through something unique. We’ve followed a distinct arc over the past 50 years: one of disillusionment. Better than most, we understand the disjunctions of our present because they happened at crucial inflection points alongside the timeline of our lives.

We were born during a period of palate-cleansing. The Vietnam War was over. President Richard Nixon had, in 1974, resigned after Watergate, a redemptive scandal that renewed people’s faith in self-government. Journalists—yes, journalists—were sex symbols. Robert Redford played Bob Woodward in All the President’s Men. And the peanut farmer Jimmy Carter, a man who campaigned teeth-first, would be elected president in the fall, having promised a new era of idealism.

I don’t remember any of this, of course, but babies like me were launched into an atmosphere of reawakened good vibes. When Time magazine commissioned the polling firm Yankelovich, Skelly & White to gauge the country’s temperature from June to September of 1976, the company found a 10 percent jump in positivity on its “state of the nation index” between those months, the most rapid increase it had seen since it began tracking the metric. The following years were also a time of crime and stagflation and the Iran hostage crisis, but at least by the indicators used by pollsters to determine collective mood, things continued to get generally sunnier into the ’80s. “The Zeitgeist has turned zesty,” Kurt Andersen wrote in a 1984 assessment of that year’s numbers. “The U.S. is at peace, and between rising employment and fading inflation, the economy is aglow. Americans are feeling more sanguine and comfortable about their country than they have felt in two decades. A rebirth of the American spirit, as Carter dearly hoped five summers ago? It sure feels like it.”

I remember this optimism and confidence. On November 9, 1989, I sat watching television with my grandfather—a Holocaust survivor who that day, and most days, had his shirt off and a captain’s hat on his head. The Berlin Wall was coming down. This happened when we bicentennial babies were 13 and highly impressionable. Look at them, my grandfather said, his voice breaking, as people pick-axed their way out of East Germany. I recall the total elation on their faces when they finally broke through, and then the bracing thought that they were trying to get to the side where I already lived.

For many young Americans in those years, a feeling of transcendence was possible. You had a sense that good fortune had placed you somewhere that everyone in the world wished they could be. At the same time, that wider world, with its crumbling empires and ethnic cleansing and genocides, seemed very far away. Even the Gulf War of the early ’90s appeared, to those of us safe at home, as a ghostly green video game playing on CNN, transmitted from somewhere hard to recognize as real.

You may not believe me when I tell you that I read Francis Fukuyama’s The End of History and the Last Man at 19, for fun, when I was a junior and living abroad in France. But I did, and then after college I went into the Peace Corps and lived in a village in Cameroon for two years. Although many of the people there thought that I was working for the CIA (I was not), I felt I was doing something uncomplicatedly wholesome, even a little patriotic.

We were 25 when 9/11 happened. I moved to New York City in October of that year, like a salmon swimming upstream—or like a salmon following a girl. Everywhere were posters of missing people. During my first days of couch surfing, New Yorkers were further terrorized by anthrax spores sent through the mail, addressed to political and media targets. That terrible fall was a hinge moment for all Americans but maybe especially for us young adults, who were also at a hinge moment in our lives, suddenly vulnerable and less innocent in new ways, feeling silly for having believed that history could have an end.

I haven’t mentioned the internet yet, but it also came around for us as adulthood hit. I got my first email address in college and accessed my inbox in the library basement at a computer lab that perpetually smelled like Doritos. It was all so new that you could forget to send a paper to a professor and then offer the excuse that the email probably just got lost. I spent a lot of time outside that library, chatting, with nothing in my hands besides a cigarette. I think I knew someone who had a beeper. We got flip phones in our 20s. We were in our early 30s when the first iPhone arrived and Facebook showed up. We were told that these were revolutionary tools. Maybe we believed this more than other people did, still being relatively young and feeling like we were being handed powerful megaphones in our prime—a chance to make change, to connect. Then the tools congealed into yet more products that would waste our hours and make us feel terrible about ourselves and our fellow citizens.

We made lives against the backdrop of distant wars, unceasing notifications popping up on our phones. The year we turned 40, Donald Trump was elected president. Four years later came COVID. Just as we were balancing more and more—perhaps children, a challenging job, ailing parents—the world seemed to conspire to keep our heads spinning. In these past few years, before we and the country hit our big milestones, we were assaulted by panicked warnings about the state of American democracy—and the future of the entire human race. What has AI been up to over the past few days? Creating new viruses and independently cyberhacking, it appears. We are less naive, though more exhausted. It has not been lost on us that the people warning that AI could lead to our extinction are the same people who invented it. This is a pattern we’re familiar with now: Technology gives us something with one hand while robbing us of something else with the other.

I’m leaving out a lot. We also had private joys and tragedies totally impervious to what America writ large was up to. But I can distinguish a progression toward an increased sense of emergency, toward alienation, toward a mournfulness that makes me read the newspaper through my fingers most days. I don’t think this is the birthday blues talking—or, if I’m honest, maybe not just the birthday blues. It’s also the metrics: about loneliness and economic stagnation and political polarization and the whole insane technological surround sound of our lives. My point is that bicentennial babies, regardless of their individual circumstances, have all been strapped into the first row of this ride.

Someone born on America’s centennial, in 1876, could well have argued that they had witnessed much more consequential change by their 50th birthday. They might have gushed about the expansion of railroads and telegraphs, about seeing the first airplanes, telephones, and radios, and then explained what it was like to face the reality that as many as 20 million people could be killed in a single war. I wouldn’t want to go head-to-head with them. Every generation has its story. But we bicentennial babies have lived through a major rupture. For all else that might be good in our lives—and I’m lucky to have a lot that’s good—this is not such an exuberant place to find ourselves at 50.

Can we imagine anyone proudly calling the babies born this year—what? semiquincentennial sprouts? A mouthful, granted. But that’s not what makes it sound strange. Behind the “bicentennial babies” moniker was a kind of hope. We would be the Americans of the future. And we would be moving toward that future not with dread but with anticipation. Whatever one’s political affiliation, people do not have much enthusiasm these days when they picture where we’re headed.

When the Pew Research Center surveyed Americans just before this year’s semiquincentennial, 59 percent of respondents said that the country’s best years were behind it. Asked to imagine the United States 50 years from now, 44 percent were pessimistic and only 28 percent were optimistic. Perhaps most telling, 27 percent chose neither option; they just felt blah. Recently, Conan O’Brian, speaking on the podcast The Rest Is History, talked about the “undiluted joy” he remembers feeling as a preteen experiencing the bicentennial. Now: “It’s very hard for some people, maybe, to just say, I’m really excited about our 250th when our current state is so divided.”

I can’t conceive of myself being around for the tricentennial—and if I did suggest living to 100, my mother might faint from all the spitting she’d have to do to ward off the evil eye. But if I do make it there, I will have lived through a third of the country’s existence. I’ll have a lot more data to work with. Will 2026 appear in retrospect as another hinge, or simply as a snapshot of us—mouths open and eyes closed, as in an amusement-park photograph—mid–free fall? Will there be self-correction or a piling-on of bad decisions? Disintegration or newfound connection? No one can really tell. Though I do know what I would like on my 50th birthday and the country’s 250th: something for us to look forward to.
